#### Numerical Example {#sec-pmc-552}

[**Calculation of principal components example**]{#sec-pmc-552-intro}

**A numerical example** may clarify the mechanics of principal component analysis.

[**Sample data set**]{#sec-pmc-552-data}

Let us analyze the following 3-variate dataset with 10 observations. Each observation consists of 3 measurements on a wafer: thickness, horizontal displacement, and vertical displacement.

$$ {\bf X} = \left[ \begin{array}{ccc}
7 & 4 & 3 \\
4 & 1 & 8 \\
6 & 3 & 5 \\
8 & 6 & 1 \\
8 & 5 & 7 \\
7 & 2 & 9 \\
5 & 3 & 3 \\
9 & 5 & 8 \\
7 & 4 & 5 \\
8 & 2 & 2
\end{array} \right] $$

```{r}
#| label: setup-pmc-552
#| code-fold: true
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)

X <- matrix(
  c(
    7, 4, 3,
    4, 1, 8,
    6, 3, 5,
    8, 6, 1,
    8, 5, 7,
    7, 2, 9,
    5, 3, 3,
    9, 5, 8,
    7, 4, 5,
    8, 2, 2
  ),
  ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE
)
X
```

[**Compute the correlation matrix**]{#sec-pmc-552-correlation}

First compute the correlation matrix.

$$ {\bf R} = \left[ \begin{array}{rrr}
1.00 & 0.67 & -0.10 \\
0.67 & 1.00 & -0.29 \\
-0.10 & -0.29 & 1.00
\end{array} \right] $$

```{r}
#| label: verify-pmc-552-correlation
#| code-fold: true
R <- cor(X)
round(R, 2)
```

[**Solve for the roots of ${\bf R}$**]{#sec-pmc-552-roots}

Next solve for the roots of ${\bf R}$, using software.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pmc-552-eigenvalues
#| tbl-cap: "Eigenvalues of the correlation matrix, with cumulative proportion of variance explained"
#| code-fold: true
eig <- eigen(R)

tibble(
  lambda = 1:3,
  value = eig$values,
  proportion = cumsum(eig$values) / 3
) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, col.names = c("$\\lambda$", "value", "proportion"), align = "rrr")
```

Notice that:

- Each eigenvalue satisfies $|{\bf R} - \lambda {\bf I}| = 0$.
- The sum of the eigenvalues $= 3 = p$, which is equal to the trace of ${\bf R}$ (i.e., the sum of the main diagonal elements).
- The determinant of ${\bf R}$ is the product of the eigenvalues.
- The product is $\lambda_1 \times \lambda_2 \times \lambda_3 = `r round(prod(eig$values), 3)`$.

```{r}
#| label: verify-pmc-552-sum-det
#| code-fold: true
sum(eig$values)
sum(diag(R))
det(R)
prod(eig$values)
```

[**Compute the first column of the ${\bf V}$ matrix**]{#sec-pmc-552-first-column}

Substituting the first eigenvalue of 1.769 and ${\bf R}$ in the appropriate equation we obtain

$$ \left[ \begin{array}{rrr}
-0.769 & 0.670 & -0.100 \\
0.670 & -0.769 & -0.290 \\
-0.100 & -0.290 & -0.769
\end{array} \right]
\left[ \begin{array}{c}
v_{11} \\ v_{21} \\ v_{31}
\end{array} \right]
=
\left[ \begin{array}{c}
0 \\ 0 \\ 0
\end{array} \right]  \, . $$

This is the matrix expression for three homogeneous equations with three unknowns and yields the first column of ${\bf V}$:  0.64  0.69  -0.34  (again, a computerized solution is indispensable).

[**Compute the remaining columns of the ${\bf V}$ matrix**]{#sec-pmc-552-remaining-columns}

Repeating this procedure for the other two eigenvalues yields the matrix ${\bf V}$.

$$ {\bf V} =
\left[ \begin{array}{rrr}
0.64  & 0.38 & -0.66 \\
0.69  & 0.10 & 0.72 \\
-0.34 & 0.91 & 0.20
\end{array} \right] $$

```{r}
#| label: verify-pmc-552-V
#| code-fold: true
# eigen() returns eigenvectors unique only up to sign; we flip columns 1
# and 3 to match the sign convention used on the original page.
V <- eig$vectors
V[, c(1, 3)] <- -V[, c(1, 3)]
round(V, 2)
```

Notice that if you multiply ${\bf V}$ by its transpose, the result is an identity matrix, ${\bf V}^T{\bf V} = {\bf I}$.

```{r}
#| label: verify-pmc-552-VtV
#| code-fold: true
round(t(V) %*% V, 4)
```

[**Compute the ${\bf L}^{1/2}$ matrix**]{#sec-pmc-552-L-sqrt}

Now form the matrix ${\bf L}^{1/2}$, which is a diagonal matrix whose elements are the square roots of the eigenvalues of ${\bf R}$. Then obtain ${\bf S}$, the factor structure, using ${\bf S} = {\bf VL}^{1/2}$.

$$ \left[ \begin{array}{rrr}
0.64  & 0.38 & -0.66 \\
0.69  & 0.10 & 0.72 \\
-0.34 & 0.91 & 0.20
\end{array} \right]
\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}
1.33  & 0    & 0 \\
0     & 0.96 & 0 \\
0     & 0    & 0.55
\end{array} \right]
=
\left[ \begin{array}{rrr}
0.85  & 0.37 & -0.37 \\
0.91  & 0.10 & 0.40 \\
-0.45 & 0.88 & 0.11
\end{array} \right] $$

```{r}
#| label: verify-pmc-552-S
#| code-fold: true
L_sqrt <- diag(sqrt(eig$values))
S <- V %*% L_sqrt
round(S, 2)
```

So, for example, 0.91 is the correlation between the second variable and the first principal component.

[**Compute the communality**]{#sec-pmc-552-communality}

Next compute the communality, using the first two eigenvalues only.

$$ {\bf SS}^T =
\left[ \begin{array}{rr}
0.85  & 0.37 \\
0.91  & 0.09 \\
-0.45 & 0.88
\end{array} \right]
\left[ \begin{array}{rrr}
0.85  & 0.91 & -0.45 \\
0.37  & 0.09 & 0.88
\end{array} \right]
=
\left[ \begin{array}{rrr}
0.8662    & 0.8140  & -0.0606 \\
0.8140    & 0.8420  & -0.3321 \\
-0.0606 & -0.3321 & 0.9876
\end{array} \right]
$$

```{r}
#| label: verify-pmc-552-communality
#| code-fold: true
S2 <- S[, 1:2]
SSt <- S2 %*% t(S2)
round(SSt, 4)
```

[**Diagonal elements report how much of the variability is explained**]{#sec-pmc-552-diagonal}

Communality consists of the diagonal elements.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pmc-552-communality
#| tbl-cap: "Communality for each variable, using the first two principal components"
#| code-fold: true
tibble(var = 1:3, communality = diag(SSt)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4, align = "rr")
```

This means that the first two principal components "explain" `r round(diag(SSt)[1]*100, 2)`% of the first variable, `r round(diag(SSt)[2]*100, 2)`% of the second variable, and `r round(diag(SSt)[3]*100, 2)`% of the third.

[**Compute the coefficient matrix**]{#sec-pmc-552-coefficient}

The coefficient matrix, ${\bf B}$, is formed using the reciprocals of the diagonals of ${\bf L}^{1/2}$.

$$ {\bf B} = {\bf VL}^{-1/2} =
\left[ \begin{array}{rrr}
0.48  & 0.40 & -1.20 \\
0.52  & 0.10 & 1.31 \\
-0.26 & 0.95 & 0.37
\end{array} \right] $$

```{r}
#| label: verify-pmc-552-B
#| code-fold: true
L_inv_sqrt <- diag(1 / sqrt(eig$values))
B <- V %*% L_inv_sqrt
round(B, 2)
```

[**Compute the principal factors**]{#sec-pmc-552-factors}

Finally, we can compute the factor scores from ${\bf ZB}$, where ${\bf Z}$ is ${\bf X}$ converted to standard score form. These columns are the *principal factors*.

$$ {\bf F} = {\bf ZB} =
\left[ \begin{array}{rrr}
0.41  & -0.69 & 0.06 \\
-2.11 & 0.07 & 0.63 \\
-0.46 & -0.32 & 0.30 \\
1.62 & -1.00 & 0.70 \\
0.70 & 1.09 & 0.65 \\
-0.86 & 1.32 & -0.85 \\
-0.60 & -1.31 & 0.86 \\
0.94 & 1.72 & -0.04 \\
0.22 & 0.03 & 0.34 \\
0.15 & -0.91 & -2.65
\end{array} \right] $$

```{r}
#| label: verify-pmc-552-F
#| code-fold: true
# Standardizing by the population (n-divisor) standard deviation, rather
# than R's default sample (n-1-divisor) standard deviation, is needed to
# reproduce the factor scores exactly.
n <- nrow(X)
means <- colMeans(X)
pop_sd <- sqrt(colSums((t(t(X) - means))^2) / n)
Z <- scale(X, center = means, scale = pop_sd)
Fmat <- Z %*% B
round(Fmat, 2)
```

::: {.callout-note}
NIST's page does not state explicitly how ${\bf X}$ is standardized to form ${\bf Z}$. Reproducing the factor scores table exactly requires standardizing with the population (divide-by-$n$) standard deviation rather than the sample (divide-by-$(n-1)$) standard deviation ordinarily used for a correlation matrix (the correlation matrix ${\bf R}$ itself is unaffected by this choice, since both standard deviations cancel in the correlation formula). We've noted this detail in the code above for anyone reproducing the calculation.
:::

[**Principal factors control chart**]{#sec-pmc-552-chart}

These factors can be plotted against the indices, which could be times. If time is used, *the resulting plot is an example of a principal factors control chart.*
